analysis: The PR touches three read-only CLI diagnostic surfaces: DoctorRunner.swift (lines 34-35, 75-76), DoctorCommand.swift (lines 358-362, 414-415) and StatusCommand.swift (lines 135-140). Each now derives two authorization values from the daemon state file. `displayedProviderAuthorization` is used for display and for the `appAttestAuthorized` pass/warn level. `currentProviderAuthorization` is passed as `removalAuthorization` to `ProviderAuthorizationReadiness.summary`. The change is purely presentational: it adds no network calls, no writes, no key or token handling, and no new inputs. `displayedProviderAuthorization` and the updated `summary` signature are defined outside the supplied evidence, so I could not confirm that the displayed variant never overstates serving permission. `appAttestAuthorized` at DoctorCommand.swift:363 and DoctorRunner.swift:36 still calls `hasCurrentAppAttestAuthorization(now:)`. It now operates on the displayed value rather than the strictly current one. If the displayed value can retain an expired or revoked grant, doctor could show a `.pass` and suppress the MDM/attestation-readiness hints (DoctorRunner.swift:65, 107; DoctorCommand.swift:382-388). This would be a diagnostic misstatement related to T-052, T-053 and T-058. It is not a serving-authorization bypass, because the coordinator enforces authorization (platform-owned) and these paths only print. No supplied evidence shows this actually happens, so I raise it as a question and not a finding. A follow-up should check the `displayedProviderAuthorization` implementation in ProviderCore. It should confirm that it never returns an expired, revoked or wrong-coordinator authorization, and that `hasCurrentAppAttestAuthorization` still enforces expiry. It should also confirm that `summary` does not print machine, account or credential identifiers beyond what StatusCommand.swift:142 already prints (machineID, unchanged). No other regressions were identified in the supplied units.
